title: How do you handle relationships between entities in a NoSQL data model?
summary: "NoSQL has no joins" oversimplifies the real answer. Learn the two real techniques — embedding and referencing — and pick per relationship, not per database.

slides.markdown:
"NoSQL has no joins" is true as a statement about query mechanics and misleading as a statement about relationships — NoSQL models relationships fine, just with two different techniques than a relational join: **embedding** (nesting related data directly inside a document) and **referencing** (storing an ID and looking it up separately).

The skill being tested is picking the right technique per relationship — not per database. This topic walks both techniques on concrete relationship shapes: one-to-few, one-to-many, and many-to-many.

Ask: **is this relationship one-to-few, one-to-many, or many-to-many, and how often does the related data change?** A blog post with three tags is a fundamentally different shape from a user with a million activity-log entries, even though both are "one-to-many" in the abstract.

Also ask whether the related data is typically read together with its parent. If you almost always fetch a post and its comments in the same request, that pulls toward embedding; if they're usually accessed independently, that pulls toward referencing.

Structure it as: **embed for one-to-few relationships with data that rarely changes and is read together; reference — fetching separately or joining in application code — for one-to-many or many-to-many relationships.** State the relationship shape first, then apply the rule.

"An order's line items are one-to-few and read together with the order every time, so I'd embed them. A post's author is one-to-many from the author's side — one user writes many posts — so I'd reference the user by ID instead of duplicating their whole profile onto every post."

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: embedding line items vs referencing an author
slides.markdown:
| | Order line items (embed) | Post author (reference) |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | One-to-few, fixed and small per order | One-to-many, one author, many posts |
| Change frequency | Rarely changes after order is placed | Author's profile can change independently, often |
| Read pattern | Always read together with the order | Author info sometimes needed, sometimes not |
| Right technique | Embed inside the order document | Reference the author's ID, look up separately |

**How to decide:** line items are frozen at order time and belong with the order; an author's identity is shared across many posts and changes independently, so duplicating it everywhere would fight every profile update.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: many-to-many tags on posts via a join collection
slides.markdown:
For many-to-many — many posts, each with many tags, each tag applied to many posts — neither pure embedding nor a single reference field works cleanly. The standard NoSQL pattern mirrors a relational join table: a separate **join collection** storing `{postId, tagId}` pairs.

Finding "all posts with this tag" or "all tags on this post" becomes two lookups instead of one join: query the join collection for matching pairs, then fetch the actual posts or tags by the IDs returned. It's more application code than a SQL join, but it models the many-to-many shape correctly without duplicating post or tag data.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the two-lookup application-side join
slides.markdown:
Fetching a post plus its author, referenced by ID, takes two round trips instead of one query:

```
1. post = db.posts.findOne({ _id: postId })
2. author = db.users.findOne({ _id: post.authorId })
3. render(post, author)
```

This "join" logic lives in the application or service layer, not the database — the database itself never combines the two collections. For a single lookup this is a small cost; the design question is whether this pattern, run at your actual request volume, adds acceptable latency or whether it's frequent enough to justify embedding a denormalized copy of the author's name instead.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Say this explicitly: **embedding is fast to read but duplicates data and complicates updates; referencing avoids duplication but pushes the join logic into application code**, where it has to be written and maintained by hand instead of expressed declaratively in a query.

Neither is universally correct — a schema with everything embedded fights every update to shared data, while a schema with everything referenced turns every read into multiple round trips. Naming which cost you're accepting, per relationship, is the actual skill this question tests.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the embedded line-items list keeps growing unbounded
slides.markdown:
This is a signal that the relationship isn't actually "one-to-few" anymore, and embedding is no longer the right call. Most document stores have a hard document size limit, and even below that limit, an unboundedly growing embedded array means every read and write to the parent document moves more data than necessary.

The fix is to switch that specific relationship to referencing — move the growing list into its own collection with a reference back to the parent — even if other, genuinely small, embedded relationships on the same entity stay embedded. The decision is per relationship, not all-or-nothing for the whole entity.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: enforcing something like a foreign-key constraint
slides.markdown:
Since most NoSQL databases don't enforce referential integrity natively, this becomes an application responsibility. Concretely: validate the referenced ID exists at write time before saving the reference, and handle the case where a referenced entity is deleted — either cascade the deletion to dependents in application code, or leave the reference and handle a missing lookup gracefully on read (returning a placeholder rather than erroring).

Name this explicitly as a cost of referencing without native constraints: the guarantee a relational foreign key gives you for free now has to be built and maintained by hand.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: embedding an unbounded, frequently-changing relationship
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll embed this relationship too — it's simpler than adding another collection and a lookup."

**Why it's wrong:** if the relationship is actually one-to-many with unbounded growth, or the embedded data changes independently and frequently, embedding means every growth or change moves or duplicates data unnecessarily, and can eventually hit a document size limit outright.

**Correct model:** apply embedding only to genuinely one-to-few, rarely-changing, read-together relationships; reference everything else, even though it costs an extra application-side lookup.

"NoSQL doesn't lack relationships, it lacks joins as a database-level operation — you model relationships with embedding or referencing instead. I'd embed one-to-few, rarely-changing data that's always read with its parent, like an order's line items. I'd reference relationships that are one-to-many, many-to-many, or where the related data changes independently, like a post's author — accepting an extra application-side lookup in exchange for not duplicating and re-syncing that data everywhere. For many-to-many, I'd use a join collection, mirroring a relational join table, and do the join in application code with two lookups."

The fuller picture of NoSQL modeling choices is in [NoSQL data models](nosql-data-models).
